title: Regular expressions and the pumping lemma
kicker: ENCT 203 · Theory of Computation · Chapter 2 (regular languages)
subtitle: A notation for exactly the languages finite automata recognise, and a test for what they cannot.

sections.title: Regular expressions
sections.body:
You have probably used a regular expression already, perhaps to search a text file. Now you will see why it works, because regular expressions are the notation for exactly the languages a finite automaton can recognise.

They use three operators: union a|b (or +), concatenation ab, and star a*. Over {0,1}, (0|1)*01 means ends in 01, and 1*(01*01*)*… means an even number of 0s. And here is the beautiful theorem that ties it together (Kleene’s theorem): a language is regular exactly when a regular expression, a DFA, or an NFA describes it. The three descriptions are interchangeable. Which expression describes binary strings ending in 01? Anything, then 01: (0|1)*01.

questions.prompt: Which expression describes binary strings ending in 01?

figures.caption: Figure 2.7.1 — Kleene’s theorem
figures.script:

[ε-NFA] as nfa #mint
[DFA] as dfa #amber
re -> nfa : Thompson construction
nfa -> dfa : subset construction
dfa -> re : state elimination");

keynotes: Regular expressions use union a|b (or +), concatenation ab and star a*.
Kleene’s theorem: a language is regular exactly when a regular expression, a DFA or an NFA describes it.

sections.title: From expression to automaton
sections.body:
How do you turn a pattern into a machine? You build it piece by piece, like Lego. This is Thompson’s construction of an ε-NFA. A single symbol is two states joined by that symbol. Union adds a new start with ε-arrows to both machines. Concatenation links the first’s accept to the second’s start by ε. Star adds ε-loops and a bypass.

The pieces are machines you can run, and the one below is the result for a*b: any number of a’s, then one b. Does a*b accept aaab? Follow the loops on a, then b to the accepting state. Yes: a a a loop in s, b moves to f and the input ends there. It accepts any number of a’s followed by a single b.

worked.why: Does a*b accept aaab? Follow the loops on a, then b to the accepting state.
Yes: a a a loop in s, b moves to f and the input ends there.

choices.text: Any string of a’s and b’s.
b, ab, aab, aaab … (any number of a’s, then one b).

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: Must end with exactly one b.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The star allows zero or more a’s.

figures.note: a*b accepts any number of a’s then one b.

accept: f
s,a -> s
s,b -> f","input":"aaab","width":600,"height":440});

keynotes: Thompson’s construction: a single symbol is two states joined by that symbol; union adds a new start with ε-arrows to both machines.
Concatenation links the first machine’s accept to the second’s start by ε; star adds ε-loops and a bypass.
a*b accepts any number of a’s then one b, such as aaab.

sections.title: Closure properties
sections.body:
What can you do to regular languages without leaving the club? Quite a lot. They are closed under union, concatenation, star, complement, intersection and reversal. Complement has a lovely trick: swap accepting and non-accepting states of a DFA. Intersection uses the product construction, running two machines side by side.

Closure gives you proofs by construction. If L is regular then so is “strings in L that are not of even length”, because you can build it from pieces already known to be regular. To build a DFA for the complement, you just flip the accepting states, as long as the DFA is complete.

questions.prompt: How do you build a DFA for the complement of a regular language?

choices.text: Swap accepting and non-accepting states (in a complete DFA).

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Every string now ends where it used to reject.

problems.prompt: Write a regular expression for binary strings containing the substring 11.

keynotes: Regular languages are closed under union, concatenation, star, complement, intersection and reversal.
Complement: swap accepting and non-accepting states of a DFA; intersection uses the product construction.

sections.title: The pumping lemma
sections.eyebrow: Proving a language is NOT regular
sections.body:
Now for the other side of the coin. How do you prove a language is not regular? You can’t test every machine, so you use a property all regular languages share. The pumping lemma says: if L is regular there is a length p such that any string s ∈ L with |s| ≥ p can be split s = xyz with |xy| ≤ p, |y| ≥ 1, and xyⁱz ∈ L for every i ≥ 0.

Why? A DFA with p states reading p symbols must repeat a state (the pigeonhole principle), so the loop in between can be repeated or removed. To prove L is not regular, pick a string that cannot be pumped.

Try L = {aⁿbⁿ}. Suppose it were regular, with pumping length p, and take s = aᵖbᵖ. Since |xy| ≤ p, y consists only of a’s. Pumping up (i = 2) gives xy²z = aᵖ⁺|ʸ|bᵖ, which has more a’s than b’s, so it is not in L. So L is not regular: it needs to count, which a finite memory cannot.

worked.why: Claim: L = {aⁿbⁿ} is not regular. Suppose it were, with pumping length p; take s = aᵖbᵖ.
Since |xy| ≤ p, y consists only of a’s. Pumping up (i = 2) gives more a’s than b’s.
So L is not regular — it needs to count, which a finite memory cannot.

questions.prompt: Why can no finite automaton recognise aⁿbⁿ?

choices.text: It would need to remember an unbounded count of a’s.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Only a fixed number of states, so some count is forgotten.

keynotes: If L is regular, there is a length p such that any s in L with |s| ≥ p splits as s = xyz with |xy| ≤ p, |y| ≥ 1 and xyⁱz in L for all i ≥ 0.
The reason is the pigeonhole principle: a DFA with p states reading p symbols must repeat a state.
For aⁿbⁿ take s = aᵖbᵖ: pumping y (all a’s) with i = 2 gives more a’s than b’s, so the language is not regular.

sections.title: Decision algorithms
sections.body:
One more reason to love regular languages: most questions about them have an answer a program can compute. Is L empty? Check whether an accepting state is reachable. Is it finite? Look for loops. Are two languages equal? Minimise both DFAs and compare. Does a string belong? Just run it.

In the figure, state c is unreachable, so the machine accepts nothing and the language is empty. To test whether a DFA’s language is empty, you ask: can I get from the start state to any accepting state? If not, it is empty.

questions.prompt: How do you test whether a DFA’s language is empty?

choices.text: Check whether any accepting state is reachable from the start.

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: Number of states does not decide it.

figures.caption: Figure 2.11.1 — emptiness check
figures.note: State c is unreachable, so this machine accepts nothing: the language is empty.
figures.script:
var lab = create("steplab", {"name":"emp","engine":"dfa","spec":"start: a
accept: c
a,0 -> b
a,1 -> a
b,0 -> b
b,1 -> b
c,0 -> c
c,1 -> c","input":"0","width":600,"height":440});

keynotes: For regular languages most questions are decidable by algorithm.
Emptiness: is an accepting state reachable? Equality: minimise both DFAs and compare; membership: just run it.
In the example state c is unreachable, so the language is empty.

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
Here is what to remember.

  • Regular expression ⇔ NFA ⇔ DFA.
  • Closed under union, concatenation, star, complement, intersection.
  • Pumping lemma shows non-regularity (aⁿbⁿ).

Try to explain the pumping lemma to a friend in two sentences. If you can, you own it.
keynotes: Regular expressions, NFAs and DFAs are equivalent.
Regular languages are closed under union, concatenation, star, complement and intersection.
The pumping lemma shows non-regularity, as for aⁿbⁿ.
